text: The cancelled expressways in Toronto were a series of planned municipal expressways in Toronto, Ontario, Canada, that were only partially built or cancelled due to public opposition. Metropolitan Toronto's system of superhighways or freeways was intended to manage suburban growth and connect to the downtown core, in conjunction with the province's developing 400-Series Highways that would link to municipalities outside Metro. However, these expressways faced strong resistance from citizens in the downtown core, who opposed the demolition of homes and parklands, air pollution, noise, and the high cost of construction. The Spadina Expressway, planned since the 1940s, was cancelled in 1971 after only partial construction. Following its cancellation, other expressway plans, including a 'ring' around the central core, were abandoned. By the 1940s, urban development had extended beyond Toronto’s borders, and the city’s planning department recognized that population growth would require development of farmlands outside the city. In 1943, the City of Toronto Planning Board developed a plan for a nine-mile radius around Yonge Street and Queen Street, including a network of superhighways. With the creation of Metropolitan Toronto (Metro) in 1953, a new level of government was established with authority to build infrastructure such as highways, sewers, and public transit, while local governments handled land use planning. Metro planned to build an extensive network of highways that crisscrossed the city, with the province covering 50% of road project costs. Metro focused on roads serving the downtown core and connecting it to the suburbs, with key routes including the "Toronto-Barrie Highway" (Highway 400) on the north-west and the Queen Elizabeth Way on the southwest. The province was already planning Highway 400 in farmland areas, and Metro would extend these highways into the city. Construction began with the Lakeshore Expressway, which connected the QEW to the downtown core; the western section opened in 1958, continued eastward as an elevated highway to York Street in 1962, and reached the Don River by 1964. During construction, it was renamed the Gardiner Expressway after Fred Gardiner, the first chair of Metro and a major supporter. The Don Valley Parkway opened between Bloor Street and Eglinton Avenue in 1961 and expanded north and south to connect with Highway 401 in the north and the Gardiner in the south. These plans were part of a larger network first proposed in 1959 and fully developed by 1966 as the official plan. The inner ring included the Crosstown east-west along Davenport connecting to the Don Valley in the east and the Highway 400 extension to the west, the Highway 400 extension down Christie and Grace Streets from Davenport to the Gardiner near Fort York, and the Gardiner and Don Valley Expressways. The outer ring consisted of Highway 401 along the north, Highway 427 on the west, the Gardiner on the south, and the Scarborough Expressway to the east, connecting the Gardiner to Highway 401 in the far east. Other links included the Richview, a shorter at-grade expressway connecting the western end of the Crosstown at the Highway 400 extension to Highway 27 further west, eventually linking to the proposed Ontario Highway 403 and the Spadina Expressway, which ran north–south and connected the middle of Highway 401 to the downtown core, ending on Spadina Avenue near the University of Toronto. By 1962, the Spadina Expressway was approved and construction began in 1963 from Wilson Avenue to Lawrence Avenue. Initially, Metro approved only the Lawrence to Wilson section, but the province would not fund it unless the full route was approved, which it was. During construction, priority was given to access to the Yorkdale Shopping Centre, which opened in 1964, allowing drivers to travel from Lawrence Avenue north to Yorkdale via a paved section. The interchange with Highway 401 was completed later. In 1961, the Crosstown was cancelled by Metro Council, though carried forward by planning officials. Toronto and Metro proposed alternate routes for Highway 400, with Toronto favouring a route along railway lines. Metro developed its official transportation plan in 1964, evaluating three concepts: a road-oriented plan that included all expressways and omitted the Spadina subway, a transit-oriented plan that included Eglinton Avenue and Queen Street subways, extended the Spadina north to Vaughan, extended the Bloor-Danforth line east into Scarborough, and included express bus routes and commuter rail, and a mixed system that included all roads but omitted a Queen Street subway. The balanced plan, expected to be implemented by 1980, was estimated to cost $1 billion to construct, with the expressway component (Crosstown, Spadina, and Gardiner and Don Valley extensions) costing $210 million. The mixed system, though the most expensive, was approved by Metro Council in December 1966. The official plan included the Crosstown again, though it was not approved for construction. Toronto rejected the Crosstown, and the Ontario government revised the city’s official plan to allow for its possible construction. Construction of the Crosstown was not expected until the 1970s. After the Spadina south to Lawrence was completed, approval was given to proceed south to Eglinton, with the process of expropriating homes and parklands beginning, though without an interchange for the Crosstown. Construction plans became a point of growing protests in the late 1960s. The Gardiner and Don Valley Parkway had initially run through industrial areas, parkland, or unused areas, generating little public concern. As the Gardiner approached the downtown core, it began demolishing long-established neighbourhoods, and the planned expressways generally ran through well-settled areas. The Spadina Expressway passed through Forest Hill, The Annex, Harbord Village, Kensington Market, and Chinatown, while the Crosstown would have created a below-grade barrier on The Annex’s northern border and run beside Rosedale, displacing a forested ravine. Jane Jacobs, a new resident in The Annex who had previously blocked the Lower Manhattan Expressway in New York City, played a key role in opposing the Spadina Expressway. With David and Nadine Nowlan, she formed the "Stop Spadina And Save Our City" group, which became a major rallying point for anti-expressway sentiment. By the late 1960s, the Spadina Expressway had become a politically 'hot' topic. By 1969, construction had reached Eglinton Avenue (though paved only to Lawrence Avenue), less than half the planned route, and had already spent almost all of its $79 million budget. Metro Toronto had to return to the Ontario Municipal Board for additional loans, which were approved in a two-to-one decision. Stop Spadina appealed, and construction was halted pending the outcome. In 1971, Premier John Robarts retired and William Davis took office, who agreed to hear the appeal. On June 3, 1971, Davis stated in the Provincial Legislature: “If we are building a transportation system to serve the automobile, the Spadina Expressway would be a good place to start. But if we are building a transportation system to serve people, the Spadina Expressway is a good place to stop. It is our determination to opt for the latter.” Davis agreed to continue funding for the TTC subway line (now Line 1 Yonge–University) and later in 1972 agreed to complete the unfinished portion of the Spadina between Eglinton and Lawrence. The debate over continuing the Spadina further south from Eglinton continued throughout the 1970s. The cancellation of the Spadina Expressway marked the end of expressway construction in Toronto. Work on other expressways in the system was abandoned. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street, where the province left it, and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive, scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway instead of a six-lane freeway. The western terminus of the Richview forms the oversized interchange between Highways 401 and 427 and Eglinton Avenue near Pearson Airport. Highway 403 was built and now connects further west to Highway 401 at a major interchange that also connects to Highway 410. Both ends of the Scarborough Expressway were built: in the east as a large interchange that quickly turns into a smaller one with Kingston Road, and in the downtown core as a several-kilometre extension of the Gardiner past the Don Valley Parkway to Leslie Street. Lands acquired for the proposed Scarborough and Richview Expressways remained in municipal ownership for another twenty years and much of it remains in public ownership today, though future uses are undetermined. In 2001, the Gardiner East extension was demolished between the Don Valley Parkway and Leslie Street, and there were plans to remove the connection to the Don Valley Parkway, as of 2021 the connection is being realigned. In subsequent decades, the Peel and York Regions have expanded significantly in population and industrial development. An extensive highway network of Highways 403, 407, 410, 427, and 404 has developed in these suburbs and remains in the provincial inventory. Metro Toronto has not built any new expressways since the Spadina cancellation, with new expressways instead constructed by the province, some later transferred to municipal control. The province revised the Belfield Expressway route to terminate at Toronto International Airport instead of crossing Malton to Brampton, expropriated the right-of-way, and opened it as Highway 409. The segment of Highway 404 in Metro Toronto was originally intended as a northern extension of the Don Valley Parkway between Sheppard Avenue and Steeles Avenue, with the province continuing it into York Region, though the province ultimately assumed the entire project. Highway 400 initially stopped at Jane Street and was later extended to Weston Road as Black Creek Drive (scaled down to a four-lane at-grade expressway) and transferred from the province to Metro Toronto upon completion in 1982. Highway 2A and a section of QEW (east of Highway 427, re-designated as part of the Gardiner) were transferred to municipal control in 1997, drawing criticism from local politicians as a financial burden. As an alternative to road construction, the city and province have expanded TTC services and GO Transit commuter rail. Although TTC ridership declined in the 1980s and 1990s, it has recently reversed the trend, setting a new record in 2008, indicating growing demand for alternatives to private vehicles. Since expressways reached capacity in the 1970s, commuting has been handled by increased transit, with only 10% of commuters using the Gardiner Expressway to get downtown, according to 2006 figures. Highway advocates, such as political candidate Abel Van Wyk, argue that expressways are necessary to meet demand from suburban growth and automobile traffic between suburbs and the downtown core, and believe new expressways are needed to reduce congestion. Opposing groups, including residents of the core, oppose expansion due to air pollution, noise, and health effects that degrade urban living standards and hinder urban growth. Transit advocates argue that transit lines have higher capacity than expressways and represent better use of government resources. Cycling advocates promote cycling routes as alternatives for commuting and recreation. Special interest groups, such as the Citizens' Transportation Alliance of Greater Toronto, advocate for expressway construction, proposing a new expressway to the northwest (likely an expansion of Black Creek Drive) and one to the east through Scarborough along a hydro corridor or an expansion of Kingston Road, and supporting the filling in of 'missing links' in the arterial road grid. The Canadian Automobile Association published a 2004 plan including a new Scarborough Expressway over Lake Ontario, new expressways and arterial roads, and the Richview Expressway, which was quickly dismissed by Toronto City Council. The City of Toronto and the Government of Ontario focus instead on transit alternatives, aiming to reduce highway dependence through improvements to the current transit network as described in the Transit City plan. In April 2009, the province announced accelerated construction of several Transit City initiatives, including an east–west Eglinton Light Rail line connecting to the airport. Line 1 was extended north to Vaughan, and the Eglinton Crosstown LRT is under construction. It is proposed that Line 1 be extended north to Richmond Hill, Line 2 east to Scarborough City Centre, Line 5 west to Toronto Pearson International Airport, and a new Ontario Line serve the core and neighbourhoods in former North York and East York. Other plans debated during municipal elections included new toll highways or expansions of existing expressways via tolling, though toll highways have been seen as political poison and no politician has included them in any election campaign. The Crosstown Expressway was a planned east–west expressway through central Toronto. Although consistently opposed by Toronto City Council, it remained in the Metro Toronto plan until it was cancelled after the Spadina cancellation. In 1944, it was first proposed and included in the City of Toronto Official Plan in 1949 as the 'north-west arm' of the Don Valley Roadway system. The highway would have connected to Highway 400 at Old Weston Road and St. Clair Avenue, proceeded south-easterly between Davenport Road and Dupont Street, entered the Rosedale Ravine to connect with the main Don Valley roadway south of the Bloor Street Viaduct at the intersection of today’s Rosedale Valley Road and Bayview Avenue, and was estimated to cost $15 million as part of a $179 million development plan. As part of the 1959 Metropolitan Toronto plan, the expressway would have connected the Highway 400 extension along an east–west route near Christie Street and Dupont Street, east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange. The expressway would continue east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through Rosedale to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961. Almost immediately, transportation officials lobbied Toronto and Metro to revive the project. In May 1962, Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford proposed the construction of the Crosstown, along with an extensive one-way street plan for downtown Toronto, arguing it would absorb Spadina traffic and eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential amenities, and encourage development. He stated that it would be folly to proceed otherwise.

An east–west route was proposed near Christie Street and Dupont Street, extending east to the Don Valley Parkway, with Highway 400 continuing south to the Gardiner Expressway. North of Spadina Road, the Spadina Expressway would have connected via an interchange, running from north of Highway 401 through the Cedarvale and Nordheimer ravines and Spadina Road, with only a partial section built and now known as Allen Road. The expressway would have continued east along a CN/CP railway corridor north of Dupont Street to Mount Pleasant Road, then cut through the Rosedale neighbourhood east of Mount Pleasant Road to connect with the Don Valley Parkway, with this section to be built through ravine parklands. The Crosstown expressway was rejected by Metro Council in December 1961 and later revived in May 1962 by Toronto Public Works Commissioner Douglas Ford, who proposed it alongside a one-way street plan for downtown to absorb Spadina Expressway traffic, eliminate the need for road widening, preserve residential areas, and encourage development; he also stated it would be folly to terminate the Spadina at anything other than a controlled-access expressway. Metro Planning Commissioner Murray Jones estimated 40,000 daily vehicles would move between Highway 400 and the Don Valley Parkway, and Metro Traffic Director Samuel Cass noted the plan would prevent heavy traffic from using residential streets in Rosedale and Moore Park. In 1964, Metro Planning Commissioner Eli Comay proposed extending Bay Street north of Davenport to connect with the Crosstown, criticizing the city for allowing an apartment development in the path of the extension; Toronto Controller William Dennison accused Comay of setting policy unilaterally, and the Toronto Board of Control rejected Comay and allowed the development to proceed. Metro Council twice instructed planners to cease work on the Crosstown, with Chairman William Allen joking that the only way to get it out of his mind was to leave the country. The Crosstown reappeared in the 1965 transportation plan and was approved by Metro Council, though the City of Toronto’s official plan had no such expressway and the Ontario Minister of Municipal Affairs rejected and rewrote that section to align with the Metro plan. The City of Toronto remained consistently opposed. Although land was acquired, the expressway was not built, though a short connecting road between the Don Valley Parkway and the Bayview Avenue Extension and Bloor Street would have likely been integrated. When the first section of the Don Valley Parkway opened from Bloor Street to Eglinton Avenue, it served as the southern terminus and remains an on/off ramp, with the unnamed roadway being a four-lane arterial with interchanges at either end, including the named 'Chester Hill' interchange. The East Metro Freeway was a proposed north–south expressway beginning at Highway 401 east of Morningside Avenue, following the Rouge River valley to Highway 407, with phase 2 extending beyond Highway 407 between the Ninth Line and York-Durham Line in Markham to Stouffville; it was a last priority for the province, with construction not planned until after the Scarborough Expressway was completed, and was not an extension of the Scarborough Expressway, as the latter’s western terminus would have been 2 kilometres (1.2 mi) west of the East Metro’s southern terminus. After the Spadina Expressway was cancelled, the Scarborough Expressway was put on hold and reviewed; with the Scarborough plan dropped, the East Metro route became less necessary and faced serious opposition from Rouge River naturalist groups, leading to its official removal from planning documents on June 1, 1994. Part of the Donald Cousens Parkway follows the East Metro Freeway route from 14th to 16th Avenue, though this arterial road now lies entirely within Markham, whereas the original Metro plan intended a terminus in Stouffville. Markham continues to seek a southern arterial connection to Highway 401, while Toronto has not rerouted Morningside Road to meet the Ninth Line at Steeles Avenue; instead, the current plan is to extend Morningside Avenue from McNicoll Avenue to Steeles Avenue just east of Tapscott Road using a private right of way and widen Steeles from just east of Markham Road to Ninth Line, with new traffic lights and a six-lane roadway to eliminate the bottleneck; a direct connection is not possible due to needing to cut across Cedar Brae Golf Club and build near the Rouge River. The Richview Expressway, named after the Richview Sideroad (now Eglinton Avenue through Etobicoke), was only partially completed due to low use and local opposition, resulting in a wide right-of-way from Black Creek Drive to Highway 427, which now includes high-speed flyover ramps at the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange originally intended for the Richview Expressway. The expressway was also known as the Hamilton Expressway because the original routing of Highway 403 (to Hamilton) was planned to terminate at the present site of the Highway 401 and Highway 427 interchange; had that routing been followed, the Richview would have been considered a municipal extension of Highway 403. However, the province realigned Highway 403 to turn north and meet Highway 401 at a new junction, also accommodating Highway 410 to Brampton, while widening Highway 401 between Highway 403 and Highway 427. A portion of the right-of-way between Highway 403 and the Richview Expressway was later used for Eastgate Parkway, which runs a short distance before curving north and terminating at Eglinton Avenue just west of Mississauga’s boundary with Etobicoke, while the rest of the corridor remained unbuilt. Lands allocated for the Richview Expressway were sold, with several apartment buildings now constructed on the old right-of-way. The corridor was revisited in the 2014 Toronto municipal election when John Tory’s SmartTrack plan proposed heavy rail, with challenger Olivia Chow highlighting the existing buildings; Tory was elected, but the heavy rail proposal was dropped in 2016 in favor of extending the Eglinton Crosstown LRT west to the city’s border with Mississauga. Although the expressway was never completed, plans included on/off ramps for the Scarborough Expressway (Gardiner Expressway Eastern Extension), which was intended to connect the Gardiner to Highway 401 at Toronto’s eastern boundary, with one segment built before public opposition halted the project. Traffic from the east would have gone directly downtown and served southeast Toronto; instead, such traffic now combines with northbound traffic on the Don Valley Parkway, where daily volumes exceed capacity, prompting ongoing proposals for new routes. The Scarborough Expressway was first conceived in the 1940s, with detailed planning beginning in 1967, and construction expected after the Spadina Expressway. Early plans had the route beside the CN route in southern Scarborough, later shifting to an eastern extension of the Gardiner along Lake Ontario’s base, following the Scarborough Bluffs, connecting to Highway 401 via Ontario Highway 2A, a short stub freeway part of the original 401 alignment. The 1967 proposal would have required demolishing 1,200 homes; after fierce opposition, the city redesigned the route in 1973, moving it entirely into the Lakeshore East CN/GO railway corridor from the Don Valley Parkway/Gardiner interchange, depressed in a deep ditch, reducing demolitions to 706 homes. This still did not satisfy east Toronto residents, who continued to oppose the plan, leading the city to shelve it in 1974. Property had been acquired by Metro Toronto, and some infrastructure, such as an overpass for roadway and railway tracks, was built, but opposition from residents, especially in eastern Toronto, caused the route to be severed from the Gardiner. The fiercest resistance came from eastern Toronto, leading to the deletion of the section beyond the Toronto/Scarborough boundary, which would have ended at Victoria Park Avenue and potentially flooded east-end neighbourhoods. Residents continued to oppose the plan and appeared before the Ontario Municipal Board each time Metro sought additional land. Metro and Scarborough continued to promote the expressway, renamed the "Scarborough Transportation Corridor," with parts of Eglinton Avenue East considered as a potential arterial to relieve Highway 401. Until the early 1990s, Metro and Scarborough maintained the plan, but by 1994 expressway development was no longer a priority. By 1996, Metro began planning to demolish the eastern end of the Gardiner Expressway, effectively ending the Scarborough Expressway/Scarborough Transportation Corridor. The intended connection between the Don River and Leslie Street was demolished in 2001, leaving only an offramp from the Gardiner to Carlaw Avenue, which was removed in 2021 to realign ramps between the Gardiner and the Don Valley Expressway. All that remains are concrete pillars from the elevated expressway to Leslie Street. Much of the land acquired across Scarborough remains vacant, with the City of Toronto conducting studies on its future use, including local streets, housing, and public parkland. Bridges along the CN/GO corridor were built with space for two lanes on either side of the railway, which are now empty and available for future rail upgrades. In the early 2000s, much of the land east of Manse Road in Scarborough was sold; the parcel between Kingston Road and Lawrence Avenue was developed into homes, as was a portion south of the railway and east of Poplar Road. A police station, Toronto Police 43 Division, was built on a parcel south of Lawrence Avenue.
